name: Constitutionalism

furtherReading.note: Careful philosophical introduction to limited government, entrenchment and judicial review.

furtherReading.note: Locke's case for consent and limited government.

furtherReading.note: Accessible overview with critics and non-Western variants.

scope: Constitutionalism as the defining sources describe it: the doctrine that a government's authority is determined and limited by a body of laws or a constitution, so as to prevent arbitrary rule (Britannica, s5; the SEP, s2, adds that its legitimacy depends on observing those limits). The sources name two traditions, political constitutionalism (mixed government, then separation of powers and representative democracy) and legal constitutionalism (entrenched rights protected by courts), and note that it is not a synonym for limited government and has no necessary link to written constitutions or judicial review (s2, s5, s6). They tie it to the social-contract thinkers (Locke), Montesquieu's separation of powers and the American founding (The Federalist). It covers procedures and limits on power; the economic, cultural and foreign-policy content of particular constitutions is outside it.

summary: Constitutionalism holds that a government's authority is determined and limited by law or a constitution, to prevent arbitrary rule. Its sources stress limits entrenched against ordinary majorities, separation of powers with mutual checks, governing by standing public laws, consent as the basis of authority and a right to resist rulers who break their trust. They say little on economic, cultural or foreign policy.
notes: Searched the SEP, Britannica, the Encyclopedia of the American Constitution entry, Locke's Second Treatise and Federalist 51 across government, liberty and means statements. It is a procedural doctrine, so most statements are null. Earlier passes' zeros that rested on adherents splitting were replaced by null.
